title: Frictions in Shadow Banking: Evidence from the Lending Behavior of Money Market Funds
research_question: Do shocks to the funding of short-term credit intermediaries propagate to unrelated borrowers, such that distress affecting one set of borrowers reduces the ability of other creditworthy firms to raise short-term financing? More broadly, do relationships between short-term lenders and borrowers create frictions that prevent seamless substitution across lenders, even for large, highly rated issuers in market-based financing?
data_description: The authors construct a novel security-level dataset of holdings of all U.S. prime money market mutual funds using SEC Form N-MFP filings, which since November 2010 require monthly portfolio disclosures. The primary sample covers November 2010 through May 2012, with most analyses focused on March–August 2011, divided into a pre-period (March–May 2011) and post-period (June–August 2011). After excluding feeder funds, internal cash-management funds, variable annuities, and prime muni funds, the sample includes 177 prime funds managing roughly $1.7 trillion. Data are aggregated to the fund-issuer-month level, covering 231 non-European issuers (ABCP, financial, nonfinancial). Key variables include fund flows, portfolio share, weighted-average maturity, gross and net yields, fund exposure to Eurozone banks (Fund Euro share), and issuer-level exposure (Issuer Euro share). Supplementary issuer-level data on long-term debt issuance, cash, commercial paper outstanding, and capital expenditures come from Capital IQ.
institutional_context: Prime money market mutual funds are a critical part of the U.S. shadow banking system and the largest holders of open-market commercial paper, providing short-term financing to financial and nonfinancial issuers. SEC Rule 2a-7 restricts these funds to highest-rated, short-maturity securities, and individual fund boards must preapprove issuers, limiting flexibility in expanding lending to new borrowers. In the spring of 2011, escalating concerns about peripheral Eurozone sovereign debt (Greece, Ireland, Portugal) raised fears about Eurozone banks holding such debt. On June 15, 2011, Moody's placed major French banks (BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole, Societe Generale) on review for downgrade citing Greek exposures. This triggered a 'slow-motion run': prime fund assets fell from $1.67 trillion on June 8 to $1.49 trillion by August 31, 2011—an 11% decline and the largest three-month drop outside the 2008 crisis. Eurozone bank holdings then represented over a quarter of prime fund assets, offering yields about 20 bps above other issuers.
